finding: --role has two distinct exit-2 paths and the spec orders only one of them, leaving the other's position in the command lifecycle unbuildable. §4.2.2 orders the mode-legality refusal: 'evaluated before the mode's own argument validation'. But §4.2.1's unknown-name refusal cannot sit there. Deciding that a name is 'recognised nowhere' requires consulting skipped_roles, and skipped_roles is only computable after the round is resolved, the corpus loaded, checklist matches computed and — under --diff-from — the spec diff taken; the exit-2 hint is defined as 'listing what the invocation would have emitted', which requires the emission to have run to completion. So the unknown-name check is necessarily a post-emission decision while the mode check is a pre-validation one, and the spec presents them as one rule. An engineer therefore has no answer for the case where both fire in a legal mode: `tp review <spec> --diff-from <bad-ref> --role <typo>` — does the bad ref fail first with its own error, or does --role produce a hint it cannot compute because the emission never ran? Neither exit code nor hint is specified.
suggestion: Split the rule explicitly in §4.2.1: the mode-legality refusal is a pre-flight check (§4.2.2's ordering), the unrecognised-name refusal runs after the emission because its hint is derived from it, and in a legal mode a failure of the mode's own arguments is reported normally and --role is never reached. One added sentence removes the guess.

finding: The exit-0 branch's only observable output is a field tp deletes under a global flag the spec never mentions, so the new rule silently breaks a shipped --compact contract. §4.2.1 fixes the recognised-but-not-emitted case as 'exits 0 with prompts: [] and the role's own entry present in skipped_roles, carrying the reason tp already computes', and §6.2 property 5 asserts that echo. But skipped_roles is an explanatory field tp strips under --compact — review.go guards it with `if !IsCompact()` and the comment reads 'an explanatory field omitted under --compact'. Verified: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --compact` emits no skipped_roles key at all. So `tp review <spec> --role <name> --compact` for a skipped role exits 0 with an empty prompts[] and nothing else — indistinguishable from a bug, from an unrecognised name that failed open, or from a round that emitted nothing. §4.2.2's table enumerates the flag's legality by mode and lists --compact in neither column, and §6.2 property 5 is unsatisfiable there. --compact is exactly the flag a token-minimising caller (P3) reaches for, so this is the combination the release's own audience will hit first.
suggestion: Rule on --compact explicitly: either exempt the --role exit-0 reason from --compact stripping (it is diagnostic, not explanatory, once the flag is present), or make the exit-0 branch carry the reason on a channel --compact keeps. Say which in §4.2.1 and scope property 5 to it.

finding: S1 fences exactly two paths — spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ — as 'byte-identical after the suite runs and unchanged throughout it', and gives the reason itself: properties 7 and 8 compare emissions across separate invocations, so an input that shifts between them 'would make those comparisons fail or pass for reasons that have nothing to do with --role'. §6.1's own closing sentence then names a second such input and does not fence it: the tp audit half 'needs a working tree with git history because it detects affected files by git diff', so the working tree is an input to every audit prompt. Property 7 holds 'for both commands', so its audit half compares one unrestricted emission against N per-role emissions while nothing forbids the tree from changing between them — a fixture the suite creates inside the repo, a build artifact, or a concurrently running test is enough to flip it. Two engineers write different suites from this text: one fences the two directories and stops, one also snapshots the working tree, and only the second is stable.
suggestion: Extend S1's 'unchanged throughout' to the working-tree state the audit half's affected-file detection reads, or scope property 7's audit half to a fixed affected-file set so the audit emission does not depend on git at all.

finding: S1 rejects the one cheap isolation mechanism on a premise that is false for one of the four items it lists, and that item is the one §6.2's largest property depends on. S1's new sentence: '--no-state is not one, because it disables the state the tests measure — the round number, skipped_roles, the consecutive-clean count and whether regression is appended'. Measured on the current binary, `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --no-state` emits `skipped_roles: []` as a present top-level key — byte-identical to the stateful run's value — because skipped_roles is computed from the corpus filters (domain, enabled:false, checklist emptiness) in buildReviewPrompts, not from review state. --no-state disables the other three; it does not disable skipped_roles. This matters beyond the factual slip: §6.2 property 5's entire exit-0 branch is an assertion about skipped_roles, and S1 discards --no-state partly on the ground that it would take that key away.
suggestion: Drop skipped_roles from the list and re-check whether the remaining three actually force the relocate-the-spec conclusion; property 5's fixtures may be buildable under --no-state, which would remove the constraint §6.1 currently calls binding.

finding: After this round's rewrite, property 3 has no assertion an implementer can write that is capable of failing on a live emission. Its live-emission half is "an emitted body's last 468 bytes are property 1's suffix" — but property 1 already fixes that suffix byte-exactly as LF LF + §2.2's clause + LF LF + §3.2's clause, and §1.1's own table gives those strings as 287 and 177 bytes, so 2+287+2+177=468 is arithmetic on property 1's literals, not an independent measurement. The clause cannot fail unless property 1 has already failed. The trailing half — "restoring that one byte reconstructs it" — names no comparison at all: nothing is stated that the reconstruction must equal, so there is no predicate to assert. The only falsifiable content property 3 ever had, the negative form, was moved to a fixture spec in the same edit. So the property an engineer is asked to implement reduces to a tautology plus a sentence with no object.
suggestion: State property 3 as the single thing that is decidable and can fail: on the fixture spec of the following paragraph, the emitted body minus its last 468 bytes contains neither clause string. Delete the length restatement (it is derivable from property 1) and delete the 'restoring that one byte reconstructs it' clause or give it an explicit equality — name what the reconstruction is compared against.

finding: Property 3's new paragraph establishes that a negative of the form 'the body contains neither clause string' is forgeable by the document under review — tp embeds changed spec sections verbatim — and therefore moves that negative onto a fixture spec that quotes neither clause. Property 2 is the structural twin of the same negative ('No prompt whose output_path is empty contains either clause') and carries no such qualification, so the hazard property 3 just fenced applies to property 2 unfenced. Property 8 pushes the suite over 'every spec in the repository', which is exactly the live-spec case property 3 was moved off, and §2.2 and §3.2 are sections of this very spec — so on any round where either changed, an emission legitimately containing the clause text would fail property 2 for a reason unrelated to the release. A QA engineer cannot tell from §6.2.1 whether property 2 is asserted on the fixture, on the repository, or on both, and the three readings give different verdicts on the same binary.
suggestion: State property 2's subject explicitly. Either say it is asserted on the same fixture spec property 3 names, or, if it must hold on live specs, replace the substring test with a non-forgeable one — e.g. the prompt does not end with §2.3's construction — since only the tail position is outside the document's control.

finding: Property 3's only falsifiable clause is now carried by a 'fixture spec' that the spec introduces in one sentence and constrains with one requirement: "The fixture spec quotes neither clause." That is not enough to build the assertion. Stripping 468 bytes from an emitted body and checking the remainder presupposes that the fixture produces at least one prompt with a non-empty output_path — the §2.3 emission predicate — and nothing here requires it. A fixture spec with no headings, no checklist matches, or one that emits only a prompt with an empty output_path, satisfies the stated requirement completely while making property 3 vacuous: it passes over an empty iteration set and reports green. This is the same shape §6.2 property 5 was faulted for and the shape §7 says the release is gated against.
suggestion: Give the fixture spec its required properties, not just its forbidden one: it must cause the invocation under test to emit at least one prompt whose output_path is non-empty, and the property must be stated over that non-empty set (or the assertion must fail when the set is empty). One sentence: 'The fixture spec emits at least one prompt with a non-empty output_path and quotes neither clause; property 3 is asserted on each such prompt.'

finding: The new fixture spec has no stated location, and both placements an implementer can choose break a constraint stated elsewhere in §6. If it lives under spec/, then invoking tp review against it creates and mutates spec/.tp-review/<base>/ — precisely the mutation S1 forbids ('spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/ are byte-identical after the suite runs and unchanged throughout it') — and it simultaneously joins property 8's subject set, which is defined as 'every spec in the repository an unrestricted invocation emits prompts for', silently enlarging the release gate's own corpus as a side effect of satisfying property 3. If it lives outside spec/, the fixture escapes both, but that is exactly the relocation §6.1 rules out when it says 'relocating the state means relocating the spec, since engine.ReviewStateDir derives the directory from the spec's own path with no override' — §6.1 presents relocation as the reason a solution is hard, never as the sanctioned mechanism. §7 separately says the four unexercised skip reasons 'must be built as fixtures', so this is not a one-off: §6 requires fixture specs in at least two places and never says where a fixture spec is allowed to live or how it satisfies S1.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §6.1 that makes fixture specs a first-class, S1-compatible category: state that fixture specs live outside spec/ (so their state directories are outside S1's forbidden set and outside property 8's iteration set), and that S1's prohibition is scoped to the repository's own spec/.tp-review/ and .tp/rounds/. Then §6.2.1's fixture and §7's skip fixtures both have a legal home.

finding: Property 5's repaired two-way partition leaves out the one mode that owns a reason, so the release's own required test case has no rule. Property 5 grants the skipped_roles echo 'in the default mode', then exempts '--perspective and --verify payloads' because they 'carry no skipped_roles key at all'. §4.2.2's table enumerates FOUR legal modes for tp review: default, --perspective, --diff-from, --verify — so the spec itself treats --diff-from as distinct from default. --diff-from is in neither branch of property 5, and it is precisely the mode that produces no-spec-change, which property 5's own closing sentence requires be 'exercised on the command that can produce it' ('no-spec-change needs --diff-from'). Measured on the shipped binary: --diff-from routes through the same default runReview path and DOES emit skipped_roles, so the echo is in fact available there — but two engineers reading property 5 will write opposite tests, one asserting the echo under --diff-from and one asserting its absence, and the round-11 repair that added the exemption is what created the gap.
suggestion: State the partition on the observable rather than the mode name: 'the reason is echoed wherever the payload carries skipped_roles; where it does not (--perspective, --verify), exit 0 with prompts: [] and no reason.' That covers --diff-from without enumerating modes and survives a mode being added.

finding: Property 12 makes 'sentence-subset' the whole verification of the only change this release makes to a key every existing review caller reads, and gives no sentence boundary. The subject is not prose: the emitted review_loop.instruction contains, verbatim, `record the round: tp review /abs/path/spec/0.36.0.md --record <findings.ndjson>. Repeat until tp review /abs/path/spec/0.36.0.md --status --check exits 0.` A period-based split shatters `0.36.0.md` into three fragments and splits the absolute path as well, so 'sentence-subset' is undecidable under the obvious implementation and produces a different verdict under every other one. §4.2.3 anticipates the neighbouring problem — it says the rule is a property rather than a list of sentences to delete because buildReviewLoopInstruction 'assembles the string across nine assignment sites' — which means tp already knows its own sentence units at construction time, and the property declines to use them.
suggestion: Define the unit the property quantifies over as the assembly unit rather than a text-level sentence: 'Under --role, review_loop.instruction is built from a subset of the assignment sites that build the unrestricted one.' That is decidable in code, needs no splitter, and matches the mechanism §4.2.3 already describes. If a text-level rule is wanted instead, pin the boundary explicitly (e.g. split on '. ' followed by an uppercase letter) so two implementations agree.

finding: §1.1 states a universal authoring rule — 'Every figure in this spec is stated with the round it was measured on, because §4 establishes that the panel and its size are round-dependent' — and §7 breaks it on all four of its figures, which are the ones carrying the release gate's entire argument. §7's dead-end paragraph asserts '145 recorded review rounds', '35 of them (24%)', '2,802 recorded rows' and '303 ... (10.8%)' with no round, date or commit. Re-measured now, from the same tree: 152 recorded review-round files, 2,973 rows, 303 without role or class = 10.2%. Three of the four figures have already drifted, inside this cycle, because this cycle's own rounds are recorded into the corpus being counted — which is the exact round-dependence §1.1 cites as the reason for the rule. §7's other measurement ('22 version specs, 5 KB to 79 KB, 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none') has the same problem: spec/.tp-review now holds 39 state directories, so the 15/7 split cannot be re-derived from the text.
suggestion: Stamp §7's figures the way §4.1 stamps its table — name the commit or the round they were measured at — or, better, state the dead ends qualitatively ('a quarter of recorded snapshots do not hash to their round's spec_hash') and keep the exact counts in the round record rather than in a document that is edited every round.

finding: The four sections modified this round spend 2,007 of their 8,243 bytes (24%) narrating drafts that no longer exist: §1.1 replaces two withdrawn anti-drift devices with 919 bytes about them (lines 46-55), property 3 adds "A draft also said the remainder 'ends with the newline §2.3 removes'", property 4 adds two rejected exception levels, property 5 adds "a draft required the echo everywhere". None of it constrains an implementation. This is the one class of spec byte whose cost is multiplied rather than paid once: measured on this round's own emission, the 'Changed sections since round 11' block is 6,579 B inside EACH of the four corpus role prompts (33% of a 20 KB prompt) and the whole spec sits inside the 88,228 B regression prompt, so retrospective prose in a modified section is re-emitted 4x every round it stays modified. §6.3 already exists as the single home for exactly this, and states the reason itself ('listed here rather than beside the properties they used to encumber, so that the properties stay readable and the reasons stay found') - but it is titled 'Dead ends, recorded once' and holds 4 rows while the document carries 24 draft-history mentions.
suggestion: Move each withdrawn construction to a one-row §6.3 entry and delete the inline narrative: §1.1's two anti-drift devices, property 3's 'ends with the newline §2.3 removes' draft, property 4's two rejected exception levels, property 5's echo-everywhere draft. Leave in each section only what an implementation must satisfy. §6.3 already claims 'recorded once' - make that claim true and this round's 24% collapses into four table rows that are never re-emitted as changed text.

finding: The emission predicate excludes an invocation tp's own emitted instruction tells the orchestrator to run every round, on the exact path §1 says §2 and §3 exist for. §2.3: 'The clauses are appended to every prompt whose output_path is non-empty, and to no other.' Measured: `tp review <spec> --perspective regression` emits one prompt with role 'regression' and output_path '' — so it carries neither clause. That invocation is not hypothetical: review_loop.instruction, emitted on every review payload, ends 'Between counted rounds, you may run tp review <spec> --perspective regression alone as an uncounted delta pass', and §4.2.3 quotes the key knowing this. The delta-pass agent is an interactively spawned sub-agent that reads the repository and writes an NDJSON findings file which is then merged — precisely the two hazards §2 (a concurrent agent mutating the tree, causing another agent's false finding) and §3 (a dying agent losing buffered rows) were written to fence. §1 says the two clauses' benefit lands on the interactive path; this is an interactive-path-only invocation the release deliberately leaves unclaused. (Distinct from the previously reported code-audit instance: that one is about a prompt that reads source; this one is about a prompt tp itself instructs the caller to run.)
suggestion: Either widen the predicate to 'every prompt a caller is instructed to execute' and give the perspective prompts an output_path, or state in §2.4 that the delta pass is knowingly unclaused and why the risk is acceptable there — the current text neither covers it nor records the exclusion.

finding: Property 3's headline claim and the paragraph added under it this round assert opposite things about how many emissions the property needs. The headline: 'The 468 bytes are the whole change, decidable from **one** emission'. The added paragraph: the negative half 'is asserted on a fixture spec, not on a live one', because a round in which §2.2 or §3.2 changed puts the clause strings in the body legitimately. So the property is decidable from one emission only if that emission comes from a second, purpose-built subject — which is two subjects, not one, and the fixture is not the artifact the release ships. The same paragraph also breaks §6's own altitude rule stated eleven lines earlier ('This section states properties, not tests ... choosing the fixtures, the harness and the assertions is a task's acceptance'): 'The fixture spec quotes neither clause' picks a fixture and constrains its content.
suggestion: Split property 3 into the part that is genuinely single-emission (the last 468 bytes equal §2.3's construction) and drop the negative half entirely — it is a uniqueness claim no single emission can carry, and §6.3 already records one withdrawn property for the same reason. Leave the fixture choice to the task.

finding: Property 3's headline — 'The 468 bytes are the whole change, decidable from one emission' — is not what its clauses establish. Its first clause, 'an emitted body's last 468 bytes are property 1's suffix', is property 1 restated: property 1 already fixes that suffix exactly, and LF LF + 287 + LF LF + 177 is 468 bytes, so the two assertions are byte-for-byte the same test. The remainder — 'the remainder is the pre-clause body with its trailing newline already removed, so restoring that one byte reconstructs it' — names a pre-clause body no test in this suite can obtain: property 9 was withdrawn for that reason and §6.3 records that a go test binary compiles one tree, so the predecessor's emitter is not callable. 'Whole change' is a two-emission claim under a one-emission label. The result is that a QA engineer writing property 3 produces either a duplicate of property 1 plus the fixture negative, or nothing new at all, and has no way to tell which of the two the spec intended.
suggestion: Drop the 'whole change' headline and state what property 3 adds over property 1 — the fixture negative on the remainder — or give the reconstruction clause a subject a single emission supplies, e.g. 'on the fixture spec, the emitted body minus its last 468 bytes contains neither clause string and does not end with LF'.

finding: Property 3's new paragraph commissions a committed fixture spec - a maintained artifact carrying a standing content constraint, 'The fixture spec quotes neither clause' - to hold one negative assertion, and the same paragraph measures the hazard it fences at zero: 'Measured on this round's own emission the count is zero, so the hazard is latent rather than live.' The assertion is also close to redundant against the positive half stated two sentences earlier: if an emitted body's last 468 bytes are property 1's suffix and the remainder plus the one restored byte is the pre-clause body, the only extra failure the string search catches is a double append, which a length fact on that same single emission already refuses. The cost is not the one paragraph. §7 already requires four purpose-built fixtures for the skip reasons the repository does not produce, and §6.1 S2 constrains what a fixture may encode; this adds another artifact class whose invariant is silently breakable - any later edit that quotes §2.2's or §3.2's clause into the fixture spec fails a test with no visible connection to the edit, which is the same forgeability the paragraph moved the assertion off a live spec to escape.
suggestion: State property 3 as a length-and-position fact decidable on any emission - the last 468 bytes equal property 1's suffix, and body length minus 468 equals the pre-clause body length - which refuses a double append without a string search a document can forge, and needs no fixture at all. If a negative form is still wanted, assert it on one of the fixtures property 5 already requires rather than commissioning another spec whose only job is to not quote two strings.

finding: Property 4 opens with an unscoped universal — '--role <name> emits exactly one prompts[] entry' — and property 5, the next item, contradicts it for a name tp recognises but the round does not emit, which 'exits 0 with prompts: []'. Property 4 states no precondition restricting it to names the round emits. So the test the text most directly licenses (for every recognised name, len(prompts) == 1) fails on exactly the case property 5 mandates, while a test that hard-codes a known-emitted name never reaches the boundary and passes whichever way the implementation resolves the conflict. Property 4's body presupposes the entry exists — 'byte-identical to that role's entry in the otherwise identical invocation without the flag' — but a presupposition is not a stated scope, and this round's edit to property 4 added an exception for review_loop.instruction without adding one for the empty-panel case.
suggestion: Scope property 4's first clause to the case it means — 'For a name the round emits, --role <name> emits exactly one prompts[] entry' — so that properties 4 and 5 partition the input space instead of overlapping on it.

finding: Two properties in §6.2 enumerate the same set of modes by two different and unlinked methods, so an implementer builds the same list twice and nothing requires the copies to agree. Property 2 derives its mode set from code — 'every --perspective value review.go validates, plus --verify — not from a list written here' — explicitly rejecting a written list. Property 6 derives the same partition from a written list: it tests refusal 'in every mode that emits none, against each command's own flag set (§4.2.2)', and §4.2.2 is a hand-maintained two-row table. A --perspective value added to review.go later is picked up automatically by property 2 and silently missed by property 6 and by §4.2.2's table, which is the drift §6.2 property 2's own wording exists to prevent.
suggestion: Apply property 2's rule to property 6: derive the legal set from what review.go and audit.go register and from whether the resulting invocation emits prompts, and demote §4.2.2's table to an illustration of the current registrations rather than the property's source. Alternatively state in §4.2.2 that the table is generated from the code by the same helper both properties use.

finding: §7's dead-end figures carry no round stamp, which §1.1 states as a rule for this document ('Every figure in this spec is stated with the round it was measured on'), and they are self-invalidating because this spec's own review loop grows the corpus they measure every round. Re-measured against the repository at round 12: '145 recorded review rounds' is now 152; '35 of them (24%)' is 35 of 152 = 23.0%; '303 of the corpus's 2,802 recorded rows (10.8%)' is 303 of 2,973 = 10.2%. Three of the five numbers no longer hold after eight rounds, and the two that do (35 and 303) hold only because they are absolute counts. A reader who re-runs the measurement and gets different numbers cannot tell whether the dead end was mis-measured or whether time simply passed, and no assertion written against these figures could stay green.
suggestion: Stamp the figures with the round they were taken at, or restate them as monotone thresholds the growing corpus cannot falsify — 'at least 35 recorded rounds, a fifth of the total, have a snapshot whose sha256 does not equal the spec_hash the round recorded' and 'at least 303 recorded rows carry no role or class' — since it is the ratios, not the counts, that decay.

finding: §1.1 mints this round's replacement anti-drift authoring rule - 'Every figure in this spec is stated with the round it was measured on' - in the same section that has just recorded two such devices failing and written 'There is no third attempt'. It is already violated where the stakes are highest. §7's four figures are the release gate's entire justification and not one names a round or a date: '145 recorded review rounds', '35 of them (24%)', '303 of the corpus's 2,802 recorded rows (10.8%)', and '22 version specs ... 15 with recorded rounds and 7 with none'. All are round-dependent by construction - this cycle appends rows to spec/.tp-review every round - and three have already moved: re-measured over spec/.tp-review just now, the repository holds 152 recorded review rounds and 2,973 rows, of which 303 (10.2%) carry no role or class. So the rule imposes a check on every future edit of this document and buys nothing, which is the exact outcome §1.1 attributes to the two devices it replaced.
suggestion: Drop the rule - the table is the derivation, and three devices in three rounds is enough evidence that a fourth will not hold - and instead pay the stamp once where it is load-bearing: give §7's four figures the round they were measured on, and record that they are re-derivable by one command over spec/.tp-review so the gate's task re-runs them rather than trusting a number the next round will move.
